title: where it comes from
subtitle: words picked up along the way

steps.prompt: what does the inner voice help with?
steps.answer: planning, remembering, and getting through hard moments.

steps.text: your inner voice didn't come out of nowhere.
this idea goes back to lev vygotsky, a psychologist in the 1930s. he watched children talk out loud while they played, and saw that talk slowly move inside.
steps.evidence: a well-known theory of how inner speech develops

steps.text: on the way in, it picks up words from the people and places around us.
does the inner voice ever sound like someone familiar?

options.label: yes
options.reply: that's common. words travel, and the kind ones do too.

options.label: no
options.reply: okay. it might be a mix of a lot of places.

options.label: that's a hard one
options.reply: that's okay. no need to go there. anything here can be skipped, and real help is in settings if it's ever wanted.

steps.text: a parent's encouragement. a teacher's red pen. a coach's push. a friend's joke.
most of those voices were trying to help, in their way. and there's room for more, including a kinder one of your own.

steps.prompt: whose kind words still come back sometimes?
steps.reply: those words are part of the inner voice too. they're worth turning up.
steps.as: i still carry kind words from {x}.

steps.text: here's the hopeful part: new words can be added, in your own voice.
the inner voice picked up words along the way. new ones can join them.
steps.evidence: a well-known theory of how inner speech develops, not tested as advice

steps.text: today, listen for one kind word the inner voice already uses.

grounding.idea: inner speech develops from the out-loud private speech of childhood
